This study examines the impact of contextual fluctuations on the
identification of semantic changes in language. We introduce a new
measure, "Contextual Variance" (CV), to assess the degree of
contextual variation that triggers semantic shifts. This measure is
derived from the outputs of a pre-trained language model. We use CV
to analyze the patterns of semantic change in the data used in the
Shift-Inference Task, a benchmark for evaluating models that
capture semantic drift. Our results show that CV significantly
correlates with the accuracy of models identifying semantic shifts,
outperforming existing measures such as KL-Divergence and
Contextual Embedding Similarity. Furthermore, we find that CV
explains the decline in performance observed at the extremes of
the semantic change spectrum. We also investigate the effect of CV
on the performance of models that learn to recognize semantic shifts,
finding that higher contextual variance leads to better performance,
and that the optimal range of CV varies across different tasks. 
Our findings suggest that the success of models identifying semantic
change is influenced by the degree of contextual variation in the
data, and that CV serves as a critical factor in this success. We
conclude that the development of more effective models for
capturing semantic drift may benefit from incorporating techniques
that enhance the model's ability to detect contextual variance.
